title: Leading across organizational boundaries
blurb: Explain how to lead people who do not report to you, across customer, supplier and partner organizations, using influence and cultural intelligence.
question: A supplier's team manager does not report to the customer's project manager or executive. How should the project manager get the work started well?

teach.h: Most of the team is not yours
teach.body: Projects are delivered by temporary teams that typically work across organizational boundaries. The project ecosystem is where the business, user and supplier ecosystems meet, and each brings its own structures, governance, culture and people. So many people on a project do not report to the project manager at all. PRINCE2 calls this leading people beyond the project's direct authority.

teach.h: What each party brings to the project
head: Party
Brings its own
rows: Goals, ways of working and culture
teach.caption: The project ecosystem is the intersection of these, so the project manager leads across several cultures at once.

teach.body: Formally, cultural intelligence is the capability to relate and work across cultures within the organizational ecosystem, and PRINCE2 says leading people beyond a project's direct authority needs a degree of it. Culture here means a group's shared attitudes, values, goals and practices. In plain English: notice how each organization and group does things, and adapt how you relate to them so you can work together.

teach.h: Leading by authority versus by influence

teach.body: A temporary leader can find authority harder to exercise, and team members may be more senior than the project manager. Asking a senior person to pull rank on someone outside their own line is likely to be ineffective. The stronger move is to build the working relationship: for example, the project manager co-creates and reviews a work package with a supplier's team manager before authorizing it.

head: Role
Relationship responsibility
rows: Interface between organizational and project ecosystems
Within the team and its interfaces with others
teach.caption: Paraphrased from the PRINCE2 7 role descriptions.

steps.label:
Shared
understanding
steps.sub: of perspectives, data and agreed knowledge

teach.caption: Manual 3.2.2: the way a project is set up should support relationship building across interfaces.

teach.h: Worked scenario: the Corran Bridge replacement
teach.body: Lowmoor County Council is replacing the Corran footbridge. Project manager Hannah Brooks leads council engineers, a design consultancy and a steel fabricator from abroad. Fabricator site lead Javier Ortiz reports to his own firm, which expects formal written instructions; the council works informally. Hannah adapts: she confirms agreements in writing, co-creates each work package with Javier and sets up a weekly joint working group. She does not ask the council's executive to 'order' Javier.

teach.text: Cultural intelligence is not only about nationality: it covers the different cultures of the organizations and groups across the ecosystem. And escalating to a senior manager to pull rank on someone outside their line is not leading across boundaries; building the relationship is.

items: Project teams are temporary and typically work across organizational boundaries (manual 3.3).
Leading people beyond the project's direct authority needs cultural intelligence: the capability to relate and work across cultures in the organizational ecosystem (manual 3.3.1).
Influence, co-creation and good working relationships matter more than position.
The board manages the interface between ecosystems; the PM manages relationships within the project ecosystem; team managers manage their team and its interfaces.
Regular meetings and working groups build shared understanding across interfaces (manual 3.2.2).

summary: You can now explain why project managers often lead people who do not report to them, define cultural intelligence, and choose influence and relationship building over borrowed authority. You can also say which roles manage which relationships across the ecosystems.

A.q: What is cultural intelligence in PRINCE2 7?
options: The ability to relate and work across cultures in the ecosystem
The shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group
The analysis of who can influence the project's success
The hidden knowledge in the project ecosystem, shared socially
A.why: Cultural intelligence is the capability to relate and work across cultures within the organizational ecosystem (manual 3.3.1).

whyNot.1: Shared attitudes, values, goals and practices define culture itself, not cultural intelligence.
whyNot.2: Identifying who can influence success or failure is stakeholder analysis in the communication management approach.
whyNot.3: Hidden knowledge shared through social learning is how the people element applies learn from experience.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Leading people beyond a project's direct authority, often across organizational boundaries, requires a degree of [?] intelligence.
options: emotional
commercial
cultural
political
A.why: PRINCE2 names cultural intelligence as needed to lead people beyond the project's direct authority (manual 3.3.1).

whyNot.0: Emotional intelligence may help, but it is not the term PRINCE2 uses here.
whyNot.1: Commercial matters are handled by the commercial management approach, not this leadership capability.
whyNot.3: 'Political intelligence' is not a PRINCE2 term.

A.q: Why does leading a project team often depend on influence rather than formal authority?
options: Project managers are barred from instructing team members
The project board holds line authority over every team member
PRINCE2 suspends team members' normal line management while a project runs
Many team members sit in other organizations and do not report to the PM
A.why: Project teams are temporary and typically work across organizational boundaries, so many people do not report to the project manager (manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

whyNot.0: The project manager does instruct work through work packages; the point is that line authority is often missing.
whyNot.1: The board directs the project but does not line-manage team members in their home organizations.
whyNot.2: Team members keep their normal line management; PRINCE2 does not suspend it.

B.q:
Which two statements about leading across organizational boundaries are correct?
1. Project teams are typically temporary and work across organizational boundaries.
2. Team members are expected to be more junior than the project manager.
3. Cultural intelligence helps people relate and work across cultures in the ecosystem.
4. Influence is unnecessary once the project board has approved the PID.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Project teams are temporary and cross boundaries (1), and cultural intelligence is the capability to relate and work across cultures (3) (manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: PRINCE2 notes it is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the project manager.
whyNot.2: Both are false: team members may be more senior, and influence remains needed throughout the project.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: approving the PID does not give the project manager line authority over other organizations' staff.

B.q: A supplier's team manager is slow to accept a work package from the customer's project manager. The PM considers asking the customer's executive to order the team manager to start. Which approach better fits PRINCE2 guidance?
options: Ask the executive, as the executive is accountable for the project
Ask the business layer to appoint a new supplier straight away
Raise an exception report so the board can direct the team manager
Build the working relationship and co-create the work package
B.why: The team manager does not report to the customer's executive, so pulling rank is unlikely to work; the project manager should build the relationship and co-create the work package (manual 3.3, 3.3.1, 16.4.1).

whyNot.0: The executive is accountable for the project, but that gives no line authority over a supplier's staff, so it does not explain the right approach.
whyNot.1: Replacing a supplier is a major commercial decision and does not address the relationship problem.
whyNot.2: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage tolerance, which has not occurred.

B.q: Which role's description includes managing relationships at the interface between the organizational ecosystem and the project ecosystem?
options: Project manager
Team manager
Project board
Project support
B.why: The project board's role description includes managing relationships at the interface of the organizational and project ecosystems.

whyNot.0: The project manager manages relationships within the project ecosystem.
whyNot.1: The team manager manages relationships within the team and its interfaces with others.
whyNot.3: Project support provides administrative services and does not hold this responsibility.

C.q: A project spans a council, a transport operator and an overseas engineering firm, each with different ways of working. The project manager adapts how she relates to each group. Which concept is she applying, and where does PRINCE2 place it?
options: Cultural intelligence, within leading successful teams
Stakeholder analysis, within the communication approach
Tailoring, within the tailor to suit the project principle
Change control, within the issues practice
C.why: Relating and working across cultures within the organizational ecosystem is cultural intelligence, covered under leading successful teams in the people element (manual 3.3.1).

whyNot.1: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is impacted or influential; it is not the capability to relate across cultures.
whyNot.2: Tailoring adapts the method to the project; adapting how she relates to people is cultural intelligence.
whyNot.3: Change control manages changes to baselines; it has nothing to do with relating across cultures.

C.q: Which pairing of a role and its relationship responsibility is correct?
options: Project manager: the interface between the two ecosystems
Team manager: relationships within the team and its interfaces
Project board: relationships within each delivery team
Project support: relationships with external suppliers
C.why: The team manager's role description includes managing relationships within the team and any interfaces with others.

whyNot.0: The interface between the organizational and project ecosystems is the project board's responsibility.
whyNot.2: Relationships within each team sit with the team manager; the board manages the interface between ecosystems.
whyNot.3: Project support provides administrative services; supplier relationships are not its role.

C.q: At Hollins Water, a working group with members from the utility, a regulator and a contractor meets regularly to agree shared data and terms. What does PRINCE2 say this builds?
options: A baseline that the change authority can then control
Independent assurance on behalf of the project board
The project's formal line-management structure
Shared understanding and relationships across interfaces
C.why: Regular meetings and working groups build relationships across interfaces and a shared understanding of perspectives, project data and agreed knowledge (manual 3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Baselines are approved products under change control; a working group builds relationships rather than a baseline.
whyNot.1: Project assurance is set up by the board and is independent of the project manager; a joint working group is not assurance.
whyNot.2: Working groups do not create line management; members keep their home reporting lines.

reteach.title: Organizing a street party
reteach.question: How do you get forty neighbours to help with a street party when none of them works for you?

blocks.h: No one reports to the organizer
blocks.body: The organizer cannot instruct anyone. Some neighbours like detailed written plans, some prefer a quick chat over the fence, and one household has very different traditions. A good organizer notices these differences, adapts how they ask, plans the day with the keenest helpers and holds a few short meetings so everyone shares the same picture. That is leading across boundaries with cultural intelligence.

blocks.text: Asking the council to order neighbours to help would not work: the council is not their boss. Relationships do the work.

explain.body: Projects are delivered by people in temporary teams that typically work across organizational boundaries, so the project manager often has no line authority over them.

test.q: Which describes a typical project team in PRINCE2?
options: A permanent team inside a single business unit
A team managed through the business's line structure
A temporary team working across organizational boundaries
A team formed and directed by the business layer
test.why: Projects are delivered by temporary teams, typically working across organizational boundaries (manual 3.3).

whyNot.0: Project teams are temporary, not permanent business-unit teams.
whyNot.1: Projects use the project management team structure, not the normal line structure.
whyNot.3: The business layer commissions the project; the board directs it and the PM manages it.

explain.body: Cultural intelligence is the capability to relate and work across cultures within the organizational ecosystem. PRINCE2 says leading people beyond the project's direct authority needs a degree of it.

test.q: Leading people beyond the project's direct authority calls for which capability?
options: Cultural intelligence
Formal line authority
Delegated change authority
Executive sponsorship
test.why: PRINCE2 says leading beyond direct authority requires a degree of cultural intelligence (manual 3.3.1).

whyNot.1: By definition, these people are beyond the project's direct authority.
whyNot.2: A change authority approves requests for change; it is not a leadership capability.
whyNot.3: 'Sponsor' is not a PRINCE2 role, and sponsorship does not create authority over other organizations' staff.

explain.body: A temporary leader can find authority harder to exercise, and team members may be more senior. Asking someone to pull rank on a person outside their line is likely to fail; building the working relationship works.

explain.h: Someone outside your line is not cooperating

test.q: A supplier's engineer does not report to the project manager. What is the project manager's main lever with the engineer?
options: Line authority over the engineer
Influence through a good working relationship
The executive's line authority over the engineer
Instructions written into the project mandate
test.why: Without line authority, the project manager leads through influence and relationships (manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

whyNot.0: The engineer reports to the supplier, so the PM has no line authority.
whyNot.2: The customer's executive does not line-manage supplier staff either.
whyNot.3: The project mandate triggers the project; it does not instruct individual supplier staff.

explain.body: The way a project is set up should support relationship building across interfaces, through regular meetings and working groups that build shared understanding of perspectives, project data and agreed knowledge.

test.q: How does PRINCE2 suggest building relationships across interfaces?
options: Regular meetings and working groups
Detailed contracts for every party
Additional management stages
Monthly exception reports
test.why: Manual 3.2.2 suggests regular meetings and working groups that build shared understanding.

whyNot.1: Contracts belong to the commercial management approach and do not by themselves build relationships.
whyNot.2: Stages are planning and decision points, not a relationship-building method.
whyNot.3: Exception reports are raised when tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not on a schedule.
